```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))

knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

library(lme4)
library(bbmle)
library(biometrydata)
library(ggplot2)

pct <- function(x){ paste0(round(100 * x), "%") }
pct1 <- function(x){ paste0(sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x), "%") }
f1 <- function(x){ sprintf("%.1f", x) }
f2 <- function(x){ sprintf("%.2f", x) }
f3 <- function(x){ sprintf("%.3f", x) }
f4 <- function(x){ sprintf("%.4f", x) }
big <- function(x){ format(round(x), big.mark = ",") }
se_of <- function(m, term){
  summary(m)$coefficients[term, 2]
}

# --- songbirds: wing shape within families ----------------------------------
songbirds <- avonet[avonet$Order1 == "Passeriformes", ]
birds <- data.frame(species = songbirds$Species1,
                    family = songbirds$Family1,
                    hwi = songbirds$Hand.Wing.Index,
                    lat = abs(songbirds$Centroid.Latitude),
                    migratory = as.numeric(songbirds$Migration == 3))
birds <- na.omit(birds)
n_birds <- nrow(birds)
n_fam <- length(unique(birds$family))

lm_lat <- lm(hwi ~ lat, data = birds)
mm_lat <- lmer(hwi ~ lat + (1 | family), data = birds)
lm_fam <- lm(hwi ~ lat + family, data = birds)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mm_lat))
sd_fam <- vc$sdcor[vc$grp == "family"]
sd_res <- vc$sdcor[vc$grp == "Residual"]
var_fam <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "family"]
var_res <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]
icc <- var_fam / (var_fam + var_res)

mm_lat_ml <- lmer(hwi ~ lat + (1 | family), data = birds, REML = FALSE)
mm_null_ml <- lmer(hwi ~ 1 + (1 | family), data = birds, REML = FALSE)
aic_vs_lm <- AIC(lm_lat) - AIC(mm_lat_ml)
aic_vs_null <- AIC(mm_null_ml) - AIC(mm_lat_ml)
ci_lat <- confint(mm_lat_ml, quiet = TRUE)

# the twelve biggest families, for the "wings run in families" figure
top_fam <- names(sort(table(birds$family), decreasing = TRUE))[1:12]
big_fams <- birds[birds$family %in% top_fam, ]
big_fams$family <- reorder(factor(big_fams$family), big_fams$hwi, median)

# shrinkage: each family's raw mean against the model's estimate
mm0 <- lmer(hwi ~ 1 + (1 | family), data = birds)
fam_n <- table(birds$family)
fam_raw <- tapply(birds$hwi, birds$family, mean)
shrink <- data.frame(family = names(fam_raw),
                     n = as.vector(fam_n[names(fam_raw)]),
                     raw = as.vector(fam_raw),
                     est = coef(mm0)$family[names(fam_raw), 1])
grand <- fixef(mm0)[[1]]
vc0 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mm0))
var_fam0 <- vc0$vcov[1]
var_res0 <- vc0$vcov[2]
keep1 <- var_fam0 / (var_fam0 + var_res0)
eup <- shrink[shrink$family == "Eupetidae", ]
tyr <- shrink[shrink$family == "Tyrannidae", ]

# --- bobwhite: the same routes, every year -----------------------------------
bw <- bobwhite_counts
bw$route <- factor(bw$route)
bw$decade <- bw$elapsed / 10
n_bw <- nrow(bw)
n_routes <- length(unique(bw$route))
max_years <- max(table(bw$route))

g_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(count ~ decade, data = bw)
mm_pois <- glmer(count ~ decade + (1 | route), family = poisson, data = bw)
mm_nb <- glmer.nb(count ~ decade + (1 | route), data = bw)
aics_bw <- c(g_nb = AIC(g_nb), mm_pois = AIC(mm_pois), mm_nb = AIC(mm_nb))
daic_bw <- aics_bw - min(aics_bw)

per_year <- function(b){ exp(b / 10) }
yr_g <- per_year(c(coef(g_nb)["decade"], confint.default(g_nb)["decade", ]))
yr_p <- per_year(c(fixef(mm_pois)["decade"],
                   confint(mm_pois, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")["decade", ]))
yr_n <- per_year(c(fixef(mm_nb)["decade"],
                   confint(mm_nb, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")["decade", ]))
decl <- function(x){ pct1(1 - x[1]) }
decl_ci <- function(x){ paste0(pct1(1 - x[3]), " to ", pct1(1 - x[2])) }

# share of counts inside each model's 95% range (Lecture 24's check)
inside <- function(lo, hi){ mean(bw$count >= lo & bw$count <= hi) }
mu_g <- fitted(g_nb)
in_g <- inside(qnbinom(0.025, mu = mu_g, size = g_nb$theta),
               qnbinom(0.975, mu = mu_g, size = g_nb$theta))
mu_p <- fitted(mm_pois)
in_p <- inside(qpois(0.025, mu_p), qpois(0.975, mu_p))
th_n <- getME(mm_nb, "glmer.nb.theta")
mu_n <- fitted(mm_nb)
in_n <- inside(qnbinom(0.025, mu = mu_n, size = th_n),
               qnbinom(0.975, mu = mu_n, size = th_n))

# how much routes differ, and which routes are left in later years
sd_route <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mm_nb))$sdcor[1]
re_route <- ranef(mm_nb)$route
bw$route_effect <- re_route[as.character(bw$route), 1]
early <- exp(mean(bw$route_effect[bw$year <= 2001]))
late <- exp(mean(bw$route_effect[bw$year >= 2015]))
routes_early <- mean(tapply(bw$route, bw$year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })[as.character(1997:2001)])
routes_late <- mean(tapply(bw$route, bw$year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })[as.character(2015:2019)])

# three routes to highlight: high, middle and low, each counted at least 15 years
long_routes <- names(which(table(bw$route) >= 15))
re_long <- re_route[long_routes, 1]
names(re_long) <- long_routes
pick <- c(names(which.max(re_long)),
          names(sort(re_long))[ceiling(length(re_long) / 2)],
          names(which.min(re_long)))
bw$show <- ifelse(as.character(bw$route) %in% pick,
                  paste("route", as.character(bw$route)), "other routes")

# random slopes: does each route decline at its own rate?
mm_slope <- glmer.nb(count ~ decade + (1 + decade | route), data = bw)
aic_slope <- AIC(mm_nb) - AIC(mm_slope)
b_slope <- fixef(mm_slope)["decade"]
sd_slope <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mm_slope))$sdcor[2]
slope_lo <- per_year(b_slope - 1.96 * sd_slope)
slope_hi <- per_year(b_slope + 1.96 * sd_slope)
route_lines <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(bw, bw$route), function(d){
  data.frame(route = d$route[1], decade = range(d$decade))
}))
route_lines$fit <- predict(mm_slope, newdata = route_lines, type = "response")

# --- your turn: migration, with families -------------------------------------
g_add <- glm(migratory ~ lat + hwi, family = binomial, data = birds)
mm_mig <- glmer(migratory ~ lat + hwi + (1 | family), family = binomial, data = birds)
or_g <- exp(coef(g_add))
or_m <- exp(fixef(mm_mig))
aic_mig <- AIC(g_add) - AIC(mm_mig)
```

Code without the label is there to watch.

::: {.notes}
Bolker 10.1 and 10.4. The point of the day: the models from the last two
lectures assume every row is independent, and most real biological data break
that, because the same site, animal or lineage shows up many times. A mixed
model is lm() or glm() plus one term that says "rows come in groups".

This is the last new statistical tool of the semester, and it is in time for
Assignment 4 (due Friday): many of their datasets have repeated sites or years.
:::

## The story so far {.smaller}

- Lecture 23: `lm()`, for normal scatter around a linear mean
- Lecture 24: `glm()`, for yes/no data and counts, through a link
- **Today:** what to do when the rows **come in groups** and are not independent

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds.
:::

# Rows that come in groups

## The same routes, every year {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(bw, aes(x = year, y = count, group = route)) +
  geom_line(data = bw[bw$show == "other routes", ], color = "grey80") +
  geom_line(data = bw[bw$show != "other routes", ], aes(color = show), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = bw[bw$show != "other routes", ], aes(color = show), size = 1.4) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#d95f02", "#1b9e77", "#7570b3")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "bobwhite counted (log scale)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Lecture 15's `r big(n_bw)` bobwhite counts come from just **`r n_routes` routes**,
each counted for up to `r max_years` years. A good route **stays** good.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The data from Lecture 15, where students estimated a decline of
2.9% a year with a negative binomial. Each grey line is one Breeding Bird Survey
route; the three colored ones are a high, a middle and a low route.

Ask the room: how many independent pieces of information are here? Not 1,360.
Two counts from the same route share its habitat, its observer and its roadside,
so knowing one tells you a lot about the other. The truth is somewhere between
100 and 1,360, and the model has to know that.

These data hold only route-years where bobwhite were seen; the zeros are in
bobwhite_occupancy (Lecture 24). That matters later.
:::

## Groups are everywhere {.smaller}

| The group | Rows within it |
|---|---|
| a survey route, a reef, a site | counted every year |
| an animal | weighed, tracked or sampled again and again |
| a plot | quadrats or seedlings within it |
| a family or genus | species that share an ancestor |
| Lecture 22's ROV dives | 729 video sections from 5 dives |

. . .

::: {.plain}
Rows from the same group are more alike than rows from different groups, so
they carry less new information than their number suggests.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Ask: does your Assignment 4 dataset have a column like this? Most
do: site, plot, individual, year, transect.

Lecture 22's notes said the ROV sections were not independent replicates, and
that a random effect for dive was the standard fix. Today is that fix. (With
only 5 dives it is not a good one; the last section says why.)

The name for analyzing grouped rows as if they were independent is
pseudoreplication (Hurlbert 1984). It is one of the most common criticisms
reviewers make of ecology papers.
:::

## Three ways to handle a group {.smaller}

| | Ignore it | A **fixed** effect | A **random** effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| in R | <code>count ~ decade</code> | <code>count ~ decade + route</code> | <code>count ~ decade + (1 &#124; route)</code> |
| estimates | nothing about routes | `r n_routes - 1` route differences | **one** number: how much routes differ |
| the catch | treats every row as independent | many parameters; nothing to say about a new route | needs enough groups (about 5 or more) |

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The middle column is what students already know: route as a
factor, like habitat in Lecture 23 or beach in Lecture 24's turtles. It is a
legitimate fix, and it was the partial fix suggested for Lecture 22's dives.

The random effect is the new idea. Instead of estimating 99 separate route
differences, it assumes the routes' differences come from one normal
distribution, and estimates that distribution's spread: one parameter. The next
slide draws it.

The fixed-effect version also cannot include anything measured at the route
level, like how developed the route is, because the route factor already uses up
every difference between routes.
:::

## What a random effect is {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
xs <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200) * sd_route
ggplot(re_route, aes(x = `(Intercept)`)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20, fill = "#9ecae1", color = "white") +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = xs, y = dnorm(xs, 0, sd_route)), aes(x = x, y = y),
            linewidth = 1, color = "#08519c") +
  labs(x = "how far each route sits above or below the average route (log scale)",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

Each route gets its **own intercept**, drawn from a **normal distribution**
centered on the average route. The model estimates that distribution's **standard
deviation**: here `r f2(sd_route)` on the log scale, so a route one standard
deviation above average has `r f1(exp(sd_route))` times the birds.

::: {.plain}
A random effect says the groups differ, and estimates how much, instead of
estimating every group separately.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The bars are the 100 routes' estimated intercepts from the model
we fit later; the curve is the normal distribution the model assumes they came
from. One parameter, the standard deviation, describes all 100.

Bolker 10.4's language: the model has two levels of variation, among routes and
among years within a route. That is why these are also called multilevel or
hierarchical models. "Mixed" means a mix of fixed effects (decade, the thing we
want to estimate) and random effects (route, the grouping).

The "random" in random effect does not mean the routes were chosen by lottery.
It means we treat them as a sample from a larger population of routes, and we
want to say something about that population.
:::

# `lmer()`: wings within families

## Wings run in families {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
ggplot(big_fams, aes(x = hwi, y = family)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#c6dbef", outlier.size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "hand-wing index (HWI): higher means a more pointed wing", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Lecture 23 fit `hwi ~ lat` across `r big(n_birds)` songbirds as if each species
were independent. But **relatives share a wing**: a swallow has pointed wings
partly because its ancestors did.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The twelve largest songbird families. Swallows (Hirundinidae) are
not among the twelve biggest, but they are the familiar example: every
swallow has long pointed wings, wherever it lives.

This is the comparative-method problem: species are not independent data points
because they share ancestry. A random effect for family is the simplest
version of the fix. The full version uses the whole phylogeny (phylogenetic
regression, for example the phylolm or MCMCglmm packages), which is beyond this
course, but the logic is the same.
:::

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(lme4)      # mixed models: install it first if you need to
library(bbmle)
library(biometrydata)

songbirds <- avonet[avonet$Order1 == "Passeriformes", ]
birds <- data.frame(species = songbirds$Species1,
                    family = songbirds$Family1,
                    hwi = songbirds$Hand.Wing.Index,
                    lat = abs(songbirds$Centroid.Latitude),
                    migratory = as.numeric(songbirds$Migration == 3))
birds <- na.omit(birds)

nrow(birds)                     # species
length(unique(birds$family))    # families
```
:::

**Check:** `r big(n_birds)` species in `r n_fam` families.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The same songbirds as Lectures 23 and 24, with one new column:
family. lme4 is the standard package for mixed models in R, written by Doug
Bates, Martin Maechler, Ben Bolker (our textbook's author) and Steve Walker.
:::

## Fit it {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# names: lm_ for lm() fits, mm_ for mixed models
lm_lat <- lm(hwi ~ lat, data = birds)                   # every species independent
mm_lat <- lmer(hwi ~ lat + (1 | family), data = birds)  # each family its own intercept

coef(lm_lat)
summary(mm_lat)
```
:::

`(1 | family)`: "an intercept (`1`) that varies by (`|`) family".

**Check:** the latitude slope drops from `r f3(coef(lm_lat)["lat"])` to
`r f3(fixef(mm_lat)["lat"])` HWI units per degree.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. lmer() is lm() with one extra piece in the formula. Everything
else (data =, the fixed part of the formula) is the same.

The bar is read "given" or "by": the intercept, by family. The next slides read
the output and then decode the bar more generally.
:::

## Reading the output {.smaller}

| From `summary(mm_lat)` | Value | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Random effects: family, Std.Dev. | `r f2(sd_fam)` | how much **families** differ in average HWI |
| Random effects: Residual, Std.Dev. | `r f2(sd_res)` | how much **species within a family** differ |
| Fixed effects: lat | `r f3(fixef(mm_lat)["lat"])` | HWI units per degree from the equator |

. . .

Square the standard deviations to get variances, and ask what share is between families:

$$\frac{`r f1(var_fam)`}{`r f1(var_fam)` + `r f1(var_res)`} = `r pct(icc)`$$

`r pct(icc)` of the variation in wing shape is **between families**: two species from
the same family are much alike.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. That share has a name, the intraclass correlation (ICC), and it is
worth reporting: it says how strongly the grouping matters. Near 0, the groups
barely differ and the mixed model will match lm(). Near 1, rows within a group
are nearly copies of each other.

No p-values in summary(): the lme4 authors left them out on purpose, because the
right degrees of freedom are not well defined for mixed models. We do not need
them; the intervals come in two slides.

If someone asks: fitting route or family as a fixed factor, lm(hwi ~ lat +
family), gives a slope of `r f3(coef(lm_fam)["lat"])`, the same as the mixed model
here, but with `r length(coef(lm_fam))` coefficients instead of 2 plus one
standard deviation.
:::

## The bar, decoded {.smaller}

| Term | Says |
|---|---|
| <code>(1 &#124; family)</code> | each family has its own **intercept** |
| <code>(1 + lat &#124; family)</code> | each family has its own intercept **and its own slope** for latitude |
| <code>(1 &#124; site/plot)</code> | plots **nested** within sites: plot 1 at site A is not plot 1 at site B |
| <code>(1 &#124; site) + (1 &#124; year)</code> | **crossed**: every site was visited in every year |

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. For Assignment 4 and the final project. Most student datasets need
only the first line. Nested is the common second case (quadrats within plots
within sites). Crossed is common in monitoring data, where the same sites are
revisited every year, and a bad year affects all sites at once.

Rule of thumb from Bolker's GLMM FAQ: start with random intercepts, add random
slopes only if the question is about whether slopes differ, and only with enough
groups and enough rows per group.
:::

## Small families borrow from big ones {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
keep <- function(n){ var_fam0 * n / (var_fam0 * n + var_res0) }
ns <- 10^seq(0, log10(max(shrink$n)), length.out = 200)
ggplot(shrink, aes(x = n, y = keep(n))) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(n = ns), color = "#08519c", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#08519c", size = 1.6, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "species in the family (log scale)",
       y = "share of its own difference
from average the model keeps") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Eupetidae has one species, with an HWI of `r f1(eup$raw)`, far below the
average of `r f1(grand)`. The model keeps only `r pct(keep1)` of that difference
and puts the family at `r f1(eup$est)`. **Small families are pulled toward the
average; big ones keep their own.**

::: {.plain}
A family with one species is mostly guesswork, so the model trusts it less and
leans on what all the other families say.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. This is called shrinkage, or partial pooling. "Ignore the
groups" pools everything together (every family gets the overall average).
"A fixed effect" pools nothing (every family gets its own raw average, however
few species). The random effect is in between, and how far each family moves
depends on how much information it has.

Eupetidae is the rail-babbler, a ground bird of New Guinea forests with very
rounded wings. The tyrant flycatchers, with `r tyr$n` species, barely move: from
`r f1(tyr$raw)` to `r f1(tyr$est)`.

The curve is var_family * n / (var_family * n + var_residual): the more species,
the more the family's own average counts. Every family sits exactly on it in
this simple model.

This figure uses a model with no latitude (hwi ~ 1 + (1 | family)), so the
raw averages and the estimates are on the same footing. coef(mm_lat)$family
gives each family's intercept from the real model.
:::

## Why did the slope change? {.smaller}

| | <code>lm(hwi ~ lat)</code> | <code>lmer(hwi ~ lat + (1 &#124; family))</code> |
|---|---|---|
| slope, HWI per degree | `r f3(coef(lm_lat)["lat"])` | `r f3(fixef(mm_lat)["lat"])` |
| standard error | `r f4(se_of(lm_lat, "lat"))` | `r f4(se_of(mm_lat, "lat"))` |

. . .

- `lm()` compares **any two species**: part of its slope is "families far from
  the equator have pointier wings"
- `lmer()` leans on comparisons **within families**: "a species that lives
  farther from the equator than its relatives has pointier wings than they do"
- Here the interval got **narrower**: family soaks up variation that was noise to
  `lm()`. Your turn shows it can go the other way.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Both slopes are positive, so the biology holds: farther from the
equator, pointier wings, which fits longer migrations. But the within-family
version is the cleaner claim, because a family-level difference could be about
anything that family shares, not latitude.

The standard error shrank because the residual standard deviation fell from
`r f2(sigma(lm_lat))` to `r f2(sd_res)`: family explains a lot of what lm() treated
as unexplained scatter. Ignoring groups does not always make you overconfident.
It makes you wrong about how confident to be, in either direction.
:::

## Compare, and get intervals {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

`lmer()` fits by **REML** by default, which gives better standard deviations but
cannot compare models with different fixed effects. For **AIC**, refit with
`REML = FALSE`.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
mm_lat_ml  <- lmer(hwi ~ lat + (1 | family), data = birds, REML = FALSE)
mm_null_ml <- lmer(hwi ~ 1 + (1 | family), data = birds, REML = FALSE)
AICtab(lm_lat, mm_null_ml, mm_lat_ml)

confint(mm_lat_ml)     # profile intervals, as in Lecture 17
```
:::

**Check:** `mm_lat_ml` wins by `r big(aic_vs_null)` over no latitude and by
`r big(aic_vs_lm)` over `lm_lat`. Slope `r f3(ci_lat["lat", 1])` to
`r f3(ci_lat["lat", 2])`.

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. REML (restricted maximum likelihood) corrects the standard
deviations for the fact that the fixed effects were estimated too, the same
reason the sample variance divides by n - 1. The price is that its likelihood
depends on the fixed effects in a way that makes AIC comparisons between
different fixed effects meaningless. So: REML = FALSE whenever you compare fixed
effects with AIC; REML (the default) for the final estimates. With 6,583 rows,
the two give nearly identical numbers.

Comparing lm_lat with mm_lat_ml is legitimate: same response, same rows, both
fit by maximum likelihood. A gap of `r big(aic_vs_lm)` says family matters a lot.

confint() profiles the likelihood, as in Lectures 17 and 21. It labels the
random effects .sig01 (the family standard deviation, `r f2(ci_lat[1, 1])` to
`r f2(ci_lat[1, 2])`) and .sigma (the residual standard deviation). It takes a
few seconds.
:::

# `glmer()`: bobwhite routes

## `glmer()` is `glm()` with groups {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Same `family =`, same link, plus a bar term. Back to the routes:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
bw <- bobwhite_counts
bw$route <- factor(bw$route)    # route numbers are names, not amounts
bw$decade <- bw$elapsed / 10    # decades since 1996: glmer() prefers numbers near 1

nrow(bw)
length(unique(bw$route))
```
:::

**Check:** `r big(n_bw)` counts on `r n_routes` routes.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. factor(route) is Lecture 23's number trap: route 56 is not "more"
than route 1. lme4 would treat a numeric grouping column as a factor anyway, but
being explicit is safer.

Decades instead of years: glmer() finds its answer by numerical optimization,
like mle2(), and it struggles when one predictor runs from 0 to 23 while the
intercept is near 2 (Lecture 20's scaling problem). With years it fits but
warns "Model is nearly unidentifiable: very large eigenvalue. Rescale
variables?". Decades fix that. We convert back to years in two slides.
:::

## Fit it {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Lecture 15's model: a negative binomial, every count independent
g_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(count ~ decade, data = bw)

# the same decline, with a random intercept for route
mm_pois <- glmer(count ~ decade + (1 | route), family = poisson, data = bw)
mm_nb <- glmer.nb(count ~ decade + (1 | route), data = bw)

AICtab(g_nb, mm_pois, mm_nb)
```
:::

**Check:** `mm_nb` wins, by `r big(daic_bw["g_nb"])` over ignoring routes and by
`r big(daic_bw["mm_pois"])` over the Poisson.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. glmer.nb() is lme4's negative binomial version, as glm.nb() is
for glm(). It is slower: it fits the model again and again to find theta.

Why the Poisson loses even with routes: routes explain part of the extra
scatter, but not all of it. Lecture 24's range check says the same: the share of
counts inside each model's 95% range is `r pct(in_g)` for g_nb, `r pct(in_p)` for
mm_pois and `r pct(in_n)` for mm_nb. Same code as Lecture 24, with fitted()
from each model (and getME(mm_nb, "glmer.nb.theta") for theta); in the
solutions.
:::

## Undo the link {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
b <- fixef(mm_nb)["decade"]    # fixef(): the fixed effects, on the log scale, per decade
exp(b)                         # birds multiplied by this per decade
exp(b / 10)                    # ... and per year

ci <- confint(mm_nb, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
exp(ci["decade", ] / 10)       # per year, with a 95% interval

exp(coef(g_nb)["decade"] / 10) # Lecture 15's answer, for comparison
```
:::

**Check:** `r f3(yr_n[1])` a year: **`r decl(yr_n)` fewer birds each year**
(`r decl_ci(yr_n)`), against `r decl(yr_g)` when routes are ignored.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Lecture 24's move: a log link, so exp() turns the coefficient into
a multiplier. Dividing by 10 before exp() turns a per-decade multiplier into a
per-year one, because exp(b)^(1/10) = exp(b / 10).

parm = "beta_" asks for the fixed effects only. method = "Wald" is the fast,
quadratic approximation (Lecture 24's 1.96 standard errors); confint(mm_nb)
without it profiles, which is better and takes about a minute here.
:::

## Why is the decline steeper? {.smaller}

| | ignore routes, `glm.nb()` | `glmer(poisson)` | `glmer.nb()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| decline per year | `r decl(yr_g)` | `r decl(yr_p)` | **`r decl(yr_n)`** |
| 95% interval | `r decl_ci(yr_g)` | `r decl_ci(yr_p)` | `r decl_ci(yr_n)` |
| inside the 95% range | `r pct(in_g)` | `r pct(in_p)` | `r pct(in_n)` |

. . .

- Routes **leave these data** when no bobwhite are seen: about `r round(routes_early)`
  routes a year in 1997 to 2001, `r round(routes_late)` in 2015 to 2019
- The routes left are the **good** ones: `r pct(late - 1)` above an average route,
  against `r pct(early - 1)` early on
- Ignoring routes, good routes in later years **hide** part of the decline. With
  a random effect, **each route is compared with itself**.

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. This is the payoff of the lecture, so slow down. The 2.9% from
Lecture 15 was not wrong arithmetic; it answered a muddier question. Across all
rows, later years are dominated by the routes that still have birds, which
makes the average count fall more slowly than the count on any one route.

The "above an average route" numbers are the route intercepts (from ranef())
averaged over the counts in each period and turned into multipliers with exp().

The Poisson mixed model gets close on the estimate but its interval is too
narrow, for the reason Lecture 24 gave: it allows too little scatter (only
`r pct(in_p)` of counts fall inside its 95% range).

Caveat worth saying: routes that lose bobwhite entirely drop out of these data,
so even the mixed model only sees the routes where birds were found. The
occupancy model in Lecture 24 handles the other half of the story.
:::

## Does each route decline at its own rate? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
mm_slope <- glmer.nb(count ~ decade + (1 + decade | route), data = bw)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(route_lines, aes(x = 1996 + 10 * decade, y = fit, group = route)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey55", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "expected count (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

AIC prefers it by `r big(aic_slope)`. The average route loses
`r pct1(1 - per_year(b_slope))` a year, but routes vary: most fall between
`r pct1(1 - slope_lo)` fewer and `r if (slope_hi > 1) paste0(pct1(slope_hi - 1), " more") else paste0(pct1(1 - slope_hi), " fewer")` birds a year.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, to watch. (1 + decade | route) gives every route its own slope as
well as its own intercept, with the slopes drawn from a normal distribution
too. That costs two more parameters (the slopes' standard deviation, and how
slopes and intercepts correlate).

The biology: some routes are being developed and some are not. Lecture 16 found
counts fall with the share of a route that is built up; a route-level predictor
like frac_built could explain why the slopes differ, and only a random effect
leaves room for it.

It takes several seconds and prints an odd internal warning from glmer.nb(),
which is why it is not type-and-run. The "most routes" range is the average
slope plus and minus 1.96 of the slopes' standard deviation.
:::

## When `lmer()` and `glmer()` complain {.smaller}

| Message | Usually means | Try |
|---|---|---|
| "very large eigenvalue: Rescale variables?" | predictors on very different scales | decades not years; `scale(x)` |
| "Model failed to converge" | the optimizer stopped early (Lecture 20) | rescale; fewer random slopes |
| "boundary (singular) fit" | a standard deviation estimated at 0 | too few groups, or that term does not vary: drop it |

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. These are the three messages they will see in Assignment 4 and the
final project. None is an error: R still returns a model, which is exactly why
they need to read the warnings rather than ignore them.

Example: lmer(hwi ~ lat + (1 + lat | family)) fails to converge with latitude
in degrees.

Bolker's GLMM FAQ (bbolker.github.io/mixedmodels-misc/glmmFAQ.html) is the
place to look. Also ?lme4::convergence and ?lme4::troubleshooting, which the
warning itself names.
:::

# Your turn

## Your turn: migration, with families {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Lecture 24's model: every species independent
g_add <- glm(migratory ~ lat + hwi, family = binomial, data = birds)

# mm_mig: the same model, plus a random intercept for family
# (hint: glmer() takes the same family = as glm())

# odds ratios side by side: exp(coef()) for g_add, exp(fixef()) for mm_mig

# standard errors: the second column of summary(...)$coefficients, for each
```
:::

**Before you fit:** with `lmer()`, family made the latitude slope's standard
error **smaller**. Will these get bigger or smaller?

**Check:** per unit of HWI, the odds ratio goes from `r f2(or_g["hwi"])` to
`r f2(or_m["hwi"])`. Both standard errors **grow**: latitude's
`r f1(se_of(mm_mig, "lat") / se_of(g_add, "lat"))` times, HWI's
`r f1(se_of(mm_mig, "hwi") / se_of(g_add, "hwi"))` times.

::: {.notes}
Ten to fifteen minutes, in pairs. The answer:

mm_mig <- glmer(migratory ~ lat + hwi + (1 | family), family = binomial, data = birds)

Odds ratios: latitude `r f3(or_g["lat"])` to `r f3(or_m["lat"])` per degree; HWI
`r f3(or_g["hwi"])` to `r f3(or_m["hwi"])` per unit. Standard errors: latitude
`r f4(se_of(g_add, "lat"))` to `r f4(se_of(mm_mig, "lat"))`, HWI
`r f4(se_of(g_add, "hwi"))` to `r f4(se_of(mm_mig, "hwi"))`.

For anyone fast: AICtab(g_add, mm_mig). Family wins by `r big(aic_mig)`.
:::

## What your turn shows {.smaller}

- **Both intervals widen.** `glm()` counted `r big(n_birds)` species as
  independent evidence; relatives are not, so it was **too sure**
- **The HWI effect doubles.** Within a family, the species with more pointed
  wings are much more likely to migrate
- **Family matters:** it wins by `r big(aic_mig)` AIC units

::: {.plain}
Ignoring groups makes a model wrong about how sure it is: sometimes too sure
(here), sometimes not sure enough (the wing-shape slope earlier).
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Why the direction differs between the two examples: in the
lmer() model, family soaked up a large share of what lm() had treated as
residual scatter (the residual standard deviation fell from
`r f2(sigma(lm_lat))` to `r f2(sd_res)`), and less scatter means a sharper slope.
A binomial model has no residual standard deviation to shrink, so the main
effect of adding family is to discount the evidence that comes from comparing
different families, and the intervals widen. The general rule for Assignment
4: a predictor measured at the group level (a site's elevation) gets roughly one
piece of information per group, so expect its interval to widen most.

Why the HWI effect grows: glmer() estimates the effect within a family, and in
a logit model a within-group effect is generally larger than the
across-everyone effect glm() estimates, because the between-family scatter
flattens glm()'s curve. Worth one sentence if someone asks why the estimate
changed so much.
:::

# Wrapping up

## Random or fixed? {.smaller}

| A **random** effect when | A **fixed** effect (a factor) when |
|---|---|
| the groups are a **sample** (routes, families, sites) | you care about **these** groups (the three beaches you manage) |
| there are **about 5 or more** groups | there are only a few (Lecture 22's 5 dives is borderline) |
| you want to say something about a **new** group | you only predict for these groups |
| something is measured **at the group level** | |

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Bolker 10.4 and the GLMM FAQ give the same advice: with fewer than
about five groups, the standard deviation among groups cannot be estimated well
(it often comes out as exactly 0, the "singular fit" warning), so a fixed effect
is the honest choice. That is why Lecture 22's five dives were handled by adding
dive as a predictor.

Year is a common hard case: a random effect if years are a sample of
weather, a fixed effect or a trend if you care about change over time. Both
can be in the same model, as here: decade as a trend, route as random.
:::

## Which tool, when {.smaller}

| Your response | Rows independent | Rows in groups |
|---|---|---|
| continuous, normal scatter | `lm()` | `lmer()` |
| yes/no, or successes out of trials | `glm(family = binomial)` | `glmer(family = binomial)` |
| counts | `glm(family = poisson)` | `glmer(family = poisson)` |
| counts with extra scatter | `MASS::glm.nb()` | `glmer.nb()` |

Compare with `AIC`, using `REML = FALSE` in `lmer()`. Intervals with `confint()`.
Undo the link as in Lecture 24.

::: {.notes}
The slide to photograph, next to Lecture 24's "Which tool, when". Each row is the
same model with one extra term.

Beyond this course, for Assignment 4 or the final project if needed: nlme's
nlme() for nonlinear mixed models (Bolker 10.4), glmmTMB for more distributions
(zero-inflated counts, beta for percentages), and Bolker 10.5 for writing a
mixed model's likelihood by hand.
:::
